claim: Independence of irrelevant alternatives is one of the assumptions of decision theory and behavioural economics.
source: Independence of irrelevant alternatives is one of the assumptions of decision theory and behavioural economics: optimally, decisions between two options should be made in the same way regardless of whether or not a third option – a distractor – is also present.
evidence: This is established knowledge in decision theory and behavioral economics.

claim: Distractors impact on the neural mechanisms underlying choice representation and decision making and alter the choices people and animals take.
source: In practice, however, several lines of evidence suggest distractors impact on the neural mechanisms underlying choice representation and decision making and, as a result, subtly but significantly, alter the choices people and animals take (Chau et al., 2014; Louie et al., 2015; Louie et al., 2011; Louie et al., 2013; Louie et al., 2014; Noonan et al., 2017; Noonan et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: The relative accuracy of decisions made between two choosable options decreases as the value of a third distractor increases.
source: First, it has been reported that the relative accuracy of decisions made between two choosable options – the frequency with which the better option is chosen -- decreases as the value of a third distractor increases.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The decrease in decision accuracy with high value distractors has been interpreted as a consequence of divisive normalisation.
source: This has been interpreted as a consequence of divisive normalisation – the representation of any option's value is normalised by the sum of the values of all options present including distractors (Chau et al., 2014; Louie et al., 2015; Louie et al., 2011; Louie et al., 2013; Louie et al., 2014; Noonan et al., 2017; Noonan et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research.

claim: In many sensory systems, neural codes are adaptive and the rate of neural activity recorded in response to a given stimulus is related to the range of other stimuli encountered in the same context.
source: The argument is bolstered by the observation that in many sensory systems, neural codes are adaptive and the rate of neural activity recorded in response to a given stimulus is related to the range of other stimuli encountered in the same context.
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research.

claim: In the context of a bright light stimulus, the neural responses to two dimmer stimuli will be more similar to one another than they would otherwise be, making it more difficult to discern the brighter of the two dim stimuli.
source: For example, in the context of a bright light stimulus that leads to a high rate of neural responding in the visual system, the neural responses to two dimmer stimuli will be more similar to one another than they would otherwise be (Carandini and Heeger, 2012). As a result, discerning the brighter of the two dim stimuli becomes more difficult.
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research.

claim: A similar normalisation process occurs during value-guided decision making when a high value distractor is present.
source: The contention is that a similar normalisation process occurs during value-guided decision making when a high value distractor is present.
evidence: This is an inference based on the analogy to sensory systems.

claim: The presence of a high value distractor can have a positive effect and lead to an increase in accuracy when deciding between two choosable options.
source: However, it has also been found that in some circumstances the presence of a high value distractor can have a positive effect and lead to an increase in accuracy when deciding between two choosable options (Chau et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research.

claim: The positive distractor effect was explained by reference to a cortical attractor model in which decisions are made when choice representations in a neural network occupy a high firing attractor state.
source: This finding was explained by reference to a cortical attractor model in which decisions are made when choice representations in a neural network occupy a high firing attractor state (Wang, 2002; Wang, 2008; Wong and Wang, 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Competition between representations of choices in the cortical attractor network is mediated by a pool of inhibitory interneurons.
source: Competition between representations of choices in the network is mediated by a pool of inhibitory interneurons.
evidence: This is a description of the cortical attractor model architecture.

claim: The activity levels of the inhibitory interneurons are driven by pools of recurrently interconnected excitatory neurons that each represents a possible choice.
source: In turn the activity levels of the inhibitory interneurons are driven by pools of recurrently interconnected excitatory neurons that each represents a possible choice.
evidence: This is a description of the cortical attractor model architecture.

claim: Increasing activity in the inhibitory interneuron pool mediating the comparison process improves decision accuracy although it may also slow decisions.
source: Increasing activity in the inhibitory interneuron pool mediating the comparison process improves decision accuracy although it may also slow decisions (Jocham et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Higher value distractors lead to more activity in the inhibitory interneuron pool, making decisions between the choosable options more accurate.
source: Because higher value distractors lead to more activity in the inhibitory interneuron pool, decisions between the choosable options are more accurate in the presence of high value distractors.
evidence: This is an inference based on the cortical attractor model.

claim: Any model in which comparison mechanisms interact makes similar predictions to the cortical attractor model regarding positive distractor effects.
source: Although the explanation was framed in terms of the cortical attractor model, any model in which comparison mechanisms interact makes similar predictions.
evidence: This is a generalization based on model properties.

claim: If decisions are modelled by a drift diffusion process, a similar prediction is made if the diffusion process proceeds for longer on trials when there is strong evidence for choosing the distractor instead.
source: For example, if decisions are modelled by a drift diffusion process, then a similar prediction is made if the diffusion process proceeds for longer on trials when there is strong evidence for choosing the distractor instead.
evidence: This is an inference based on drift diffusion model properties.

claim: Initiating a response towards the distractor and then inhibiting it takes a finite amount of time, allowing additional time for the comparison between the choosable options to proceed concurrently.
source: This is because initiating a response towards the distractor and then inhibiting it takes a finite amount of time. This allows additional time for the comparison between the choosable options to proceed concurrently and, hence, the better of the two choosable options is more likely to be taken.
evidence: This is an inference based on the temporal dynamics of decision processes.

claim: Task manipulations that allow more time for the comparison process make the 'correct' choice more likely to emerge from the comparison process and be chosen.
source: Other task manipulations that allow more time for the comparison process, for example by simply providing an opportunity for a second decision, after there has been time for more evidence accumulation, also make the 'correct' choice more likely to emerge from the comparison process and be chosen (Resulaj et al., 2009; van den Berg et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Gluth et al., 2018 reported a series of experiments in which they claim there is no evidence of either divisive normalisation or positive distractor effects.
source: Gluth et al., 2018, however, have recently reported a series of experiments in which they claim there is no evidence of either divisive normalisation or positive distractor effects.
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Divisive normalisation and positive distractor effects are not 'opposing results'.
source: First, we explain how divisive normalisation and positive distractor effects are not 'opposing results' as is sometimes claimed (Gluth et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a claim the authors make based on their analysis.

claim: It is possible for both divisive normalisation and positive distractor effects to co-exist within the same data set but to predominate in different parts of the decision space.
source: We explain how it is possible for both effects to co-exist within the same data set but to predominate in different parts of the decision space.
evidence: This is a claim the authors make based on their analysis.

claim: Re-analysis of Gluth et al., 2018 data shows that both divisive normalisation and positive distractor effects are robustly and consistently present.
source: Second, we re-analyse Gluth et al., 2018 data and show that both divisive normalisation and positive distractor effects are robustly and consistently present.
evidence: This is based on the authors' re-analysis of existing data.

claim: Re-analysis of previously published data (Chau et al., 2014) confirms both divisive normalisation and positive distractor effects are present.
source: Similarly re-analysis of other previously published data (Chau et al., 2014) again confirms both effects are present.
evidence: This is based on the authors' re-analysis of existing data.

claim: A new data set collected at a third site exhibits both divisive normalisation and positive distractor effects.
source: In addition we report a new data set, collected at a third site, which again exhibits both effects.
evidence: This is based on new experimental data collected by the authors.

claim: The impact of larger distractor values flips from being facilitative (positive distractor effect) for gains to being disruptive (negative distractor effect) for losses.
source: We find that the impact of larger distractor values flips from being facilitative (positive distractor effect) for gains to being disruptive (negative distractor effect) for losses while the divisive normalisation effect continues to manifest in the same direction (negative distractor effect) as originally shown for gains.
evidence: This is based on experimental data from the loss experiment.

claim: The divisive normalisation effect continues to manifest in the same direction (negative distractor effect) for both gains and losses.
source: We find that the impact of larger distractor values flips from being facilitative (positive distractor effect) for gains to being disruptive (negative distractor effect) for losses while the divisive normalisation effect continues to manifest in the same direction (negative distractor effect) as originally shown for gains.
evidence: This is based on experimental data from the loss experiment.

claim: Divisive normalisation effects are truly related to the value of the distractor.
source: This pattern of results suggests that divisive normalisation effects are truly related to the value of the distractor while the positive distractor effect is related to both the distractor's value and salience (its unsigned value – the size of its value regardless of whether it is positive or negative).
evidence: This is an inference based on the pattern of results from the loss experiment.

claim: The positive distractor effect is related to both the distractor's value and salience.
source: This pattern of results suggests that divisive normalisation effects are truly related to the value of the distractor while the positive distractor effect is related to both the distractor's value and salience (its unsigned value – the size of its value regardless of whether it is positive or negative).
evidence: This is an inference based on the pattern of results from the loss experiment.

claim: Sometimes people choose the distractor itself even if this runs contrary to task instructions, termed attentional capture effects.
source: Finally, we consider a third consequence of the presence of a distractor; sometimes people choose the distractor itself even if this runs contrary to task instructions. Such choices have been termed attentional capture effects (Gluth et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Attentional capture effects exist in other data sets.
source: Again we show that such attentional capture effects exist in other data sets.
evidence: This is based on the authors' analysis of existing data.

claim: The existence of attentional capture effects is not mutually exclusive with either positive distractor or divisive normalisation effects.
source: However, we also show that the existence of attentional capture effects is not mutually exclusive with either positive distractor or divisive normalisation effects.
evidence: This is based on the authors' analysis of data.

claim: Whether or not attentional capture by the distractor occurs is itself subject to similar positive distractor and divisive normalisation effects.
source: In fact, whether or not attentional capture by the distractor occurs is itself subject to similar positive distractor and divisive normalisation effects.
evidence: This is based on the authors' analysis of data.

claim: A relationship exists between the attentional capture effect and the positive distractor effect; positive distractor effects are particularly prominent after attentional capture by the distractor.
source: In a final experiment we use eye tracking data to demonstrate that in fact a relationship exists between the attentional capture effect and the positive distractor effect; positive distractor effects are particularly prominent after attentional capture by the distractor.
evidence: This is based on eye tracking data from the final experiment.

claim: The positive distractor effect can be linked to other situations in which the provision of a greater opportunity for evidence accumulation and comparison leads to more accurate decision making.
source: This makes it possible to link the positive distractor effect to other situations in which the provision of a greater opportunity for evidence accumulation and comparison leads to more accurate decision making, for example when allowing participants extra time to revise their initial decisions (Resulaj et al., 2009; van den Berg et al., 2016).
evidence: This is an inference linking the current findings to prior research.

claim: The mutual inhibition model involves three pools of excitatory neurons that receive noisy input from the HV, LV and distractor options that compete via a common pool of inhibitory neurons.
source: In brief, it involves three pools of excitatory neurons that receive noisy input from the HV, LV and distractor (D) options that compete via a common pool of inhibitory neurons (Figure 1a).
evidence: This is a description of the model architecture shown in Figure 1a.

claim: When the distractor value is relatively large, the mutual inhibition model makes more accurate choices.
source: When the distractor value is relatively large (left-to-right), the model makes more accurate choices (brighter colors).
evidence: This is based on the model simulation results shown in Figure 1b.

claim: The mutual inhibition model exhibits a positive D-HV effect (β = 0.296, t104 = 231.858, p<10−142).
source: Consistent with the pattern in Figure 1b, the results show that the model exhibits a positive D-HV effect (β = 0.296, t104 = 231.858, p<10−142; Figure 1d).
evidence: This is based on GLM analysis of the model simulation data.

claim: The mutual inhibition model exhibits a positive HV-LV effect (β = 0.697, t104 = 663.224, p<10−189).
source: There was also a positive HV-LV effect (β = 0.697, t104 = 663.224, p<10−189) and a positive (HV-LV)(D-HV) effect (β = 0.094, t104 = 83.377, p<10−96).
evidence: This is based on GLM analysis of the model simulation data.

claim: The mutual inhibition model exhibits a positive (HV-LV)(D-HV) effect (β = 0.094, t104 = 83.377, p<10−96).
source: There was also a positive HV-LV effect (β = 0.697, t104 = 663.224, p<10−189) and a positive (HV-LV)(D-HV) effect (β = 0.094, t104 = 83.377, p<10−96).
evidence: This is based on GLM analysis of the model simulation data.

claim: The divisive normalisation model involves only two pools of excitatory neurons that receive input from either the HV or LV option.
source: Alternatively, a divisive normalisation model involves only two pools of excitatory neurons that receive input from either the HV or LV option.
evidence: This is a description of the model architecture shown in Figure 1e.

claim: In the divisive normalisation model, the input of each option is normalised by the value sum of all options (i.e. HV+LV+D), such that the distractor influences the model's evidence accumulation at the input level.
source: The input of each option is normalised by the value sum of all options (i.e. HV+LV+D), such that the distractor influences the model's evidence accumulation at the input level.
evidence: This is a description of the model architecture shown in Figure 1e.

claim: The divisive normalisation model predicts that larger distractor values will have a negative effect on decision accuracy.
source: Unlike the mutual inhibition model, the divisive normalisation model predicts that larger distractor values (left-to-right side) will have a negative effect (darker colours) on decision accuracy.
evidence: This is based on the model simulation results shown in Figure 1f.

claim: The divisive normalisation model exhibits a negative D-HV effect (β = −0.277, t104 = −229.713, p<10−141).
source: When applying GLM1a, the results show that the model exhibits a negative D-HV effect (β = −0.277, t104 = −229.713, p<10−141; Figure 1h).
evidence: This is based on GLM analysis of the model simulation data.

claim: The divisive normalisation model exhibits a positive HV-LV effect (β = 0.694, t104 = 598.596, p<10−185).
source: There were also a positive HV-LV effect (β = 0.694, t104 = 598.596, p<10−185) and a negative (HV-LV)(D-HV) effect (β = −0.094, t104 = −71.658, p<10−89).
evidence: This is based on GLM analysis of the model simulation data.

claim: The divisive normalisation model exhibits a negative (HV-LV)(D-HV) effect (β = −0.094, t104 = −71.658, p<10−89).
source: There were also a positive HV-LV effect (β = 0.694, t104 = 598.596, p<10−185) and a negative (HV-LV)(D-HV) effect (β = −0.094, t104 = −71.658, p<10−89).
evidence: This is based on GLM analysis of the model simulation data.

claim: Multiple brain structures have been identified with decision making and they likely compete to select choices with one system predominating in some situations and another system in other situations.
source: To demonstrate this, we designed a dual route model, which is inspired by the fact that multiple brain structures have been identified with decision making. It is likely that they compete to select choices with one system predominating in some situations and another system in other situations.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about brain systems involved in decision making.

claim: The intraparietal sulcus (IPS) carries decision-related signals in many situations.
source: For example, in many situations, the intraparietal sulcus (IPS) carries decision-related signals (Glimcher, 2002; Gold and Shadlen, 2007; Hanks et al., 2006; O'Shea et al., 2007; Platt and Glimcher, 1999; Shadlen and Kiani, 2013; Shadlen and Newsome, 1996)
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Decision-related signals in IPS remain present even when there is limited time in which to act.
source: and unlike decision-related signals elsewhere in the brain they remain present even when there is limited time in which to act (Jocham et al., 2014)
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Decision-related signals in IPS remain present when decisions have become easy because of over-training.
source: or when decisions have become easy because of over-training (Grol et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Divisive normalisation is present in activity recorded in IPS.
source: Moreover, divisive normalisation is present in activity recorded in IPS (Chau et al., 2014; Louie et al., 2011; Louie et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Ventromedial prefrontal cortex (vmPFC) has activity that is decision-related.
source: Another region with activity that is similarly decision-related is ventromedial prefrontal cortex (vmPFC) (Boorman et al., 2009; Chau et al., 2014; De Martino et al., 2013; FitzGerald et al., 2009; Hunt et al., 2012; Lopez-Persem et al., 2016; Noonan et al., 2010; Papageorgiou et al., 2017; Wunderlich et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: In contrast to IPS, the impact of divisive normalisation in vmPFC is less prominent or absent.
source: However, in contrast to IPS, the impact of divisive normalisation in vmPFC is less prominent or absent (Chau et al., 2014)
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research.

claim: vmPFC activity diminishes with task practice.
source: vmPFC activity diminishes with task practice (Hunt et al., 2012)
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research.

claim: vmPFC is only engaged when more time is available to make the decision.
source: and it is only engaged when more time is available to make the decision (Jocham et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research.

claim: VmPFC lesions particularly disrupt the most difficult decisions but have less impact on easier ones.
source: VmPFC lesions particularly disrupt the most difficult decisions but have less impact on easier ones (Noonan et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Lesions of vmPFC increase the impact of divisive normalisation in decision making.
source: The fact that lesions of vmPFC increase the impact of divisive normalisation in decision making (Noonan et al., 2017; Noonan et al., 2010) suggests divisive normalisation effects are mediated by a different region of the brain, such as IPS, and are perhaps even mitigated by the operation of vmPFC.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Divisive normalisation effects are mediated by a different region of the brain, such as IPS, and are perhaps even mitigated by the operation of vmPFC.
source: The fact that lesions of vmPFC increase the impact of divisive normalisation in decision making (Noonan et al., 2017; Noonan et al., 2010) suggests divisive normalisation effects are mediated by a different region of the brain, such as IPS, and are perhaps even mitigated by the operation of vmPFC.
evidence: This is an inference based on the lesion data.

claim: The dual route model comprises both mutual inhibition and divisive normalisation models as components.
source: Based on these observations from vmPFC and IPS, the dual route model comprises both mutual inhibition and divisive normalisation models as components (Figure 1i).
evidence: This is a description of the model architecture shown in Figure 1i.

claim: In the dual route model, evidence is accumulated independently in the two component models.
source: The evidence is accumulated independently in the two component models.
evidence: This is a description of the model architecture.

claim: In the dual route model, a choice is made once one of the component models has accumulated sufficient evidence.
source: A choice is made once one of the component models has accumulated sufficient evidence.
evidence: This is a description of the model architecture.

claim: The dual route model's decision accuracy pattern looks very similar to the empirical data produced by human participants reported in Figure 2c of Chau et al., 2014.
source: Interestingly, when the model's decision accuracy is plotted in Figure 1j, the pattern looks very similar to the empirical data produced by human participants reported in Figure 2c of Chau et al., 2014.
evidence: This is a comparison between model predictions and empirical data.

claim: In the dual route model, on hard trials the decision accuracy increases as a function of the relative distractor value.
source: On hard trials (Figure 1k, bottom) the decision accuracy increases as a function of the relative distractor value
evidence: This is based on the model simulation results shown in Figure 1k.

claim: In the dual route model, on easy trials the decision accuracy decreases as a function of the relative distractor value.
source: whereas on easy trials (Figure 1k, top) the decision accuracy decreases as a function of the relative distractor value.
evidence: This is based on the model simulation results shown in Figure 1k.

claim: The dual route model exhibits a significant negative (HV-LV)(D-HV) interaction effect on decision accuracy (β = −0.047, t104 = −32.195, p<10−55).
source: The results of GLM1a indeed revealed a significant negative (HV-LV)(D-HV) interaction effect on decision accuracy (β = −0.047, t104 = −32.195, p<10−55).
evidence: This is based on GLM analysis of the model simulation data.

claim: The dual route model exhibits a positive HV-LV effect (β = 0.728, t104 = 526.591, p<10−179).
source: Finally, there was a positive HV-LV effect (β = 0.728, t104 = 526.591, p<10−179) and an absence of D-HV main effect (β <0.001, t104 = 0.218, p=0.828; Figure 1i).
evidence: This is based on GLM analysis of the model simulation data.

claim: The dual route model exhibits an absence of D-HV main effect (β <0.001, t104 = 0.218, p=0.828).
source: Finally, there was a positive HV-LV effect (β = 0.728, t104 = 526.591, p<10−179) and an absence of D-HV main effect (β <0.001, t104 = 0.218, p=0.828; Figure 1i).
evidence: This is based on GLM analysis of the model simulation data.

claim: In the dual route model, on hard trials, when the distractor value becomes larger, the errors made by the mutual inhibition component decrease more rapidly in frequency than the increase in errors made by the divisive normalisation component, resulting in a net positive distractor effect.
source: On hard trials, when the distractor value becomes larger, the errors made by the mutual inhibition component decrease more rapidly in frequency than the increase in errors made by the divisive normalisation component, resulting in a net positive distractor effect.
evidence: This is based on analysis of the model components shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: In the dual route model, on easy trials when the distractor value becomes larger the decrease in errors made by the mutual inhibition model is much less than the increase in errors made by the divisive normalisation model.
source: In contrast, on easy trials when the distractor value becomes larger the decrease in errors made by the mutual inhibition model is much less than the increase in errors made by the divisive normalisation model.
evidence: This is based on analysis of the model components shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: In Experiment 1 fMRI2014, when decisions are difficult (HV-LV is small) then high value D-HV is associated with higher relative accuracy in choices between HV and LV.
source: In both data sets, when decisions are difficult (HV-LV is small) then high value D-HV is associated with higher relative accuracy in choices between HV and LV; for example, the bottom rows of Figure 3a and c turn from black/dark red to yellow moving from left to right, indicating decisions are more accurate.
evidence: This is based on the empirical data shown in Figure 3a.

claim: In Experiment 2 Gluth4, when decisions are difficult (HV-LV is small) then high value D-HV is associated with higher relative accuracy in choices between HV and LV.
source: In both data sets, when decisions are difficult (HV-LV is small) then high value D-HV is associated with higher relative accuracy in choices between HV and LV; for example, the bottom rows of Figure 3a and c turn from black/dark red to yellow moving from left to right, indicating decisions are more accurate.
evidence: This is based on the empirical data shown in Figure 3c.

claim: In Experiment 1 fMRI2014, when decisions were easy (HV-LV is large) then the positive distractor effect is much less prominent or even reverses.
source: However, when decisions were easy (HV-LV is large) then the effect is much less prominent or even reverses as would be predicted if divisive normalisation becomes more important in this part of the decision space.
evidence: This is based on the empirical data shown in Figure 3a.

claim: In Experiment 1 fMRI2014, there was a negative (HV-LV)(D-HV) effect (β = −0.243, t20 = −3.608, p=0.002).
source: In Experiment 1 fMRI2014, the results showed that the critical (HV-LV)(D-HV) effect was negative (β = −0.243, t20 = −3.608, p=0.002; Figure 3b).
evidence: This is based on GLM analysis of the empirical data.

claim: In Experiment 1 fMRI2014, there was a positive main effect of HV-LV (β = 0.738, t20 = 8.339, p<10−7).
source: There was also a positive main effect of HV-LV (β = 0.738, t20 = 8.339, p<10−7) and no main effect of D-HV (β = 0.046, t20 = 0.701, p=0.491).
evidence: This is based on GLM analysis of the empirical data.

claim: In Experiment 1 fMRI2014, there was no main effect of D-HV (β = 0.046, t20 = 0.701, p=0.491).
source: There was also a positive main effect of HV-LV (β = 0.738, t20 = 8.339, p<10−7) and no main effect of D-HV (β = 0.046, t20 = 0.701, p=0.491).
evidence: This is based on GLM analysis of the empirical data.

claim: In Experiment 2 Gluth4, there was a negative (HV-LV)(D-HV) effect (β = −0.068, t43 = −2.043, p=0.047).
source: Similarly in Experiment 2 Gluth4, there was a negative (HV-LV)(D-HV) effect (β = −0.068, t43 = −2.043, p=0.047; Figure 3d).
evidence: This is based on GLM analysis of the empirical data.

claim: In Experiment 2 Gluth4, there was a strong positive D-HV effect (β = 0.122, t43 = 5.067, p<10−5).
source: Interestingly, there was also a strong positive D-HV effect (β = 0.122, t43 = 5.067, p<10−5), suggesting that even though the distractor effect varied as a function of difficulty level, the effect was generally positive in these participants.
evidence: This is based on GLM analysis of the empirical data.

claim: In Experiment 2 Gluth4, there was a positive HV-LV effect (β = 0.571, t43 = 15.159, p<10−18).
source: There was a positive HV-LV effect (β = 0.571, t43 = 15.159, p<10−18).
evidence: This is based on GLM analysis of the empirical data.

claim: In Experiment 3 Hong Kong, there was a significant (HV-LV)(D-HV) effect (β = −0.089, t39 = −2.242, p=0.031).
source: There was a significant (HV-LV)(D-HV) effect (β = −0.089, t39 = −2.242, p=0.031).
evidence: This is based on GLM analysis of the empirical data.

claim: In Experiment 3 Hong Kong, there was a positive D-HV effect (β = 0.207, t39 = 5.980, p<10−6).
source: Again there was a positive D-HV effect (β = 0.207, t39 = 5.980, p<10−6) and a positive HV-LV effect (β = 0.485, t39 = 12.448, p<10−14).
evidence: This is based on GLM analysis of the empirical data.

claim: In Experiment 3 Hong Kong, there was a positive HV-LV effect (β = 0.485, t39 = 12.448, p<10−14).
source: Again there was a positive D-HV effect (β = 0.207, t39 = 5.980, p<10−6) and a positive HV-LV effect (β = 0.485, t39 = 12.448, p<10−14).
evidence: This is based on GLM analysis of the empirical data.

claim: Data collected under the same conditions in 105 participants at all three sites are very similar and a positive distractor effect consistently recurs when decisions are difficult.
source: It is clear that data collected under the same conditions in 105 participants at all three sites are very similar and that a positive distractor effect consistently recurs when decisions are difficult.
evidence: This is a summary of the empirical findings across experiments.

claim: When data from Experiments 1-3 are aggregated, the (HV-LV)(D-HV) interaction (β = −0.101, t104 = −4.366, p<10−4), D-HV (β = 0.223, t104 = 6.400, p<10−8) and HV-LV (β = 0.529, t104 = 20.775, p<10−38) effects were all collectively significant.
source: Next, we aggregated the data collected from the three sites and repeated the same GLM to confirm that the (HV-LV)(D-HV) interaction (β = −0.101, t104 = −4.366, p<10−4), D-HV (β = 0.223, t104 = 6.400, p<10−8) and HV-LV (β = 0.529, t104 = 20.775, p<10−38) effects were all collectively significant.
evidence: This is based on GLM analysis of the aggregated empirical data.

claim: The dual route model provided the best account of the participants' behaviour when Experiments 1–3 were considered as a whole (estimated frequency Ef = 0.898; exceedance probability Xp = 1.000).
source: Interestingly, the dual route model provided the best account of the participants' behaviour when Experiments 1–3 were considered as a whole (estimated frequency Ef = 0.898; exceedance probability Xp = 1.000, Figure 3g–h)
evidence: This is based on Bayesian model selection analysis.

claim: The dual route model provided the best account of the participants' behaviour when individual experiments were considered separately (Experiment 1: Ef = 0.843, Xp = 1.000; Experiment 2: Ef = 0.924, Xp = 1.000; Experiment 3: Ef = 0.864, Xp = 1.000).

evidence: This is based on multinomial logistic regression analysis.

evidence: This is a summary of the empirical findings across experiments.

claim: When decisions are difficult (HV-LV is small) then high value as opposed to low value distractors robustly and consistently lead to an increase in accuracy in the same data sets.
source: When decisions are difficult (HV-LV is small) then high value as opposed to low value distractors robustly and consistently lead to an increase in accuracy in the same data sets.
evidence: This is a summary of the empirical findings across experiments.

claim: While the divisive normalisation effect is related to the distractor value on easy trials and the positive distractor effect is related to the distractor value on hard trials, an additional positive distractor effect is also related to the salience of distractor on both hard and easy trials.
source: While the divisive normalisation effect is related to the distractor value on easy trials and the positive distractor effect is related to the distractor value on hard trials, an additional positive distractor effect is also related to the salience of distractor on both hard and easy trials.
evidence: This is a summary of the findings from the loss experiment.

claim: When participants make decisions between options associated with losses, the presence of more appealing distractor options (i.e. those associated with less loss) are also less salient.
source: When participants make decisions between options associated with losses, the presence of more appealing distractor options (i.e. those associated with less loss) are also less salient.
evidence: This is an inference based on the loss experiment design.

claim: On easy trials in the loss experiment, the distractors exert a combination of a value-based divisive normalization effect and a salience-based distractor effect that results in a particularly strong negative effect on accuracy.
source: On easy trials (Figure 6c, left panel, top rows) the distractors exert a combination of a value-based divisive normalization effect and a salience-based distractor effect (i.e. the reverse of the 'positive distractor effect') that results in a particularly strong negative effect on accuracy.
evidence: This is an inference based on the loss experiment data.

claim: On hard trials in the loss experiment, the distractors exert a combination of a value-based positive distractor effect and a salience-based effect that result in a particularly weak effect on accuracy.
source: In contrast, on hard trials (Figure 6c, left panel, bottom rows) the distractors exert a combination of a value-based positive distractor effect and a salience-based effect (i.e. reversed 'positive distractor effect') that result in a particularly weak effect on accuracy.
evidence: This is an inference based on the loss experiment data.

claim: Positive distractor effects may be a consequence of interactions not just between the representations of choosable options in neural networks but interactions between these representations and the representation of the distractor.
source: Positive distractor effects may be a consequence of interactions not just between the representations of choosable options in neural networks but interactions between these representations and the representation of the distractor.
evidence: This is a theoretical interpretation of the findings.

claim: If the inhibitory interneurons mediating the decision process are more active, then the evidence accumulation process is extended and decisions are less influenced by the noise.
source: Such effects are less likely to occur when the inhibitory interneurons mediating the decision process are more active, so that the evidence accumulation process is extended and decisions are less influenced by the noise.
evidence: This is based on the cortical attractor model.

claim: Individuals with higher levels of inhibitory neurotransmitters such as gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA) in vmPFC/mOFC are more accurate.
source: Sometimes the inhibitory interneuron pool is more active simply because of an individual difference; individuals with higher levels of inhibitory neurotransmitters such as gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA) in vmPFC/mOFC are more accurate (Jocham et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research.

claim: The inhibitory interneuron pool will be more active when the distractor has a high value.
source: The inhibitory interneuron pool will also be more active when the distractor has a high value (Chau et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Allowing participants more time to consider a decision, by giving them a later opportunity to revise their initial decision, also leads to greater accuracy.

evidence: Supported by citations to prior research.

source: Different mechanisms operate on different time scales (Meder et al., 2017; Wittmann et al., 2016)
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research.

evidence: Supported by citations to prior research.

source: and are anatomically placed to exert different types of influence on behaviour (Hunt and Hayden, 2017; Rushworth et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The positive distractor effect may be particularly associated with vmPFC/mOFC.
source: The positive distractor effect may be particularly associated with vmPFC/mOFC.
evidence: This is an inference based on neuroimaging and lesion data.

claim: Activity in vmPFC/mOFC reflects the key decision variable – the difference in value between choosable options – during decision making.
source: Activity in vmPFC/mOFC reflects the key decision variable – the difference in value between choosable options – during decision making (Basten et al., 2010; Boorman et al., 2009; Chau et al., 2014; De Martino et al., 2013; Fouragnan et al., 2019; Hunt et al., 2012; Lim et al., 2011; Lopez-Persem et al., 2016; Papageorgiou et al., 2017; Philiastides et al., 2010; Strait et al., 2014; Wunderlich et al., 2012).

evidence: Supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Individual variation in the size of the neural effect in vmPFC/mOFC is related to individual variation in the size of the positive distractor effect in behaviour.
source: Moreover, individual variation in the size of the neural effect is related to individual variation in the size of the positive distractor effect in behaviour (Figure 5 in Chau et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research.

source: VmPFC/mOFC lesions leave both macaques and human patients more vulnerable to the disruptive effects of distractors that are predicted by divisive normalisation (Noonan et al., 2017; Noonan et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research.

source: Both lesion and neuroimaging experiments suggest that vmPFC/mOFC is especially important in novel as opposed to over-trained decisions and in decisions involving multi-attribute options (Fellows, 2006; Hunt et al., 2012; Papageorgiou et al., 2017).
